Get those three right and a single person can eat well all week without throwing half of it away.

## Plan around ingredients, not recipes

Most meal plans list seven dinners. For one person, that is the wrong unit. A better plan starts with three or four fresh ingredients for the week and gives each one two or three jobs.

Take a cabbage. On Monday a quarter of it becomes a crunchy slaw with carrot and lime. On Wednesday another quarter is shredded into a stir-fry. On Saturday the rest goes into a soup with lentils. One vegetable, three dinners that taste nothing alike, and nothing left over.

Good candidates for this are the ingredients that last well and change character depending on how you cook them:

- **Cabbage, carrots and broccoli**, which keep for a week or more in the salad drawer.
- **Peppers and courgettes**, which can be eaten raw, roasted or stirred into pasta.
- **Eggs**, which turn any leftover vegetable into a meal in ten minutes.
- **A pulse or grain**, which stretches everything else.

{{products: green-cabbage, crown-broccoli, sweet-snacking-carrots}}

> **Tip:** Before you shop, write down the three fresh things you will buy and next to each one, two ways you will use it. If you cannot think of a second use, buy a smaller amount or pick something else.

## Portion before it goes in the fridge

Portioning is the step that saves the most food, and it takes five minutes when you unpack the shopping. The idea is simple: turn a family-sized pack into single meals straight away, while everything is fresh.

1. **Meat and fish.** Split packs into single portions. Keep what you will cook in the next day or two in the fridge, at or below 5 °C, and freeze the rest flat in labelled bags on the same day. Do it well before the "use by" date, not on it.
2. **Bread.** Slice it and freeze most of the loaf. Toast slices straight from frozen.
3. **Herbs.** Chop what you will not use this week and freeze it in a little oil.
4. **Cheese.** Grate half a block and freeze it in a bag. It melts perfectly from frozen onto pasta or toast.

Chicken thigh fillets are especially good for this. They come in manageable sizes, freeze well and stay juicy when cooked, so a single pack can become four separate dinners.

{{products: chicken-thigh-fillets, mature-cheddar}}

![A cotton tote packed with carrots, leeks, cabbage and onions](/images/editorial/tote-of-veg.jpg "Hardy vegetables are the friend of a small household: they wait for you.")

## Cook once, eat twice, freeze once

The most useful habit for one person is to cook a dish that makes three portions. You eat one that night. One goes in the fridge for lunch or dinner within the next two days. One goes in the freezer for a night when you cannot face cooking.

The rules that keep this safe are few, but they matter:

- Cool leftovers quickly and get them into the fridge or freezer within two hours of cooking. Spreading food out in a shallow container helps it cool faster.
- Eat fridge leftovers within two days.
- Keep the freezer at −18 °C. Freezing keeps food safe, but its quality slowly drops, so aim to eat frozen meals within about three months.
- Reheat until piping hot all the way through, and reheat only once.

Soups, stews, curries, chilli and pasta sauces all work well for this. Rice and pasta are better cooked fresh, since they take minutes. If you do keep cooked rice, cool it fast and eat it within a day.

For a lighter version of this approach, [batch cooking for people who hate batch cooking](/journal/batch-cooking-for-people-who-hate-batch-cooking) builds a week from three simple parts.

## Shop small without paying more

Buying loose and buying small can cost more per kilo, but only if you would have eaten the whole large pack. Most single people do not. Paying slightly more per kilo for exactly what you need is usually cheaper than buying a bigger bag and throwing a third away.

A few ways to shop small well:

- **Buy loose fruit and vegetables** by the piece: two peppers, three apples, one courgette.
- **Buy the big pack only for things that freeze or keep.** Oats, rice, lentils, frozen peas and frozen berries are all fine in bulk.
- **Shop twice a week if you can**, or once a week with a smaller top-up. Fresh food bought for three days is eaten. Fresh food bought for seven often is not.
- **Use the freezer for your vegetables too.** Frozen peas and spinach are picked and frozen quickly and are ready whenever you are.

{{products: frozen-garden-peas, puy-lentils}}

Puy lentils earn a place on this list. They cook in about 20 minutes, hold their shape, and a small bag makes many single portions: warm with roast vegetables, cold in a salad, or stirred into soup.

![A smiling woman holding a double handful of fruit and vegetables](/images/editorial/handful-of-produce.jpg "Buy only what you can hold in two hands, and you will use all of it.")

## A sample week for one

Here is how a week can look with just a cabbage, a pack of chicken thighs, a bag of lentils, a few peppers and a box of eggs:

1. **Monday:** roast chicken thigh with peppers and lentils. Cook two extra thighs.
2. **Tuesday:** the extra chicken, sliced cold into a cabbage and carrot slaw.
3. **Wednesday:** omelette with the last roast peppers and grated cheese.
4. **Thursday:** lentil and cabbage soup. Make three portions and freeze two.
5. **Friday:** pasta with frozen peas, garlic, olive oil and cheese.
6. **Saturday:** a frozen soup from the stash, with toast.
7. **Sunday:** the last of the cabbage, stir-fried with egg and rice.

Nothing is repeated, nothing is thrown out, and the freezer holds a spare dinner for next week.

## Your next step

On your next shop, pick three fresh ingredients and give each one two jobs before you put it in the basket. Portion the meat as soon as you get home. You will likely throw away less by the end of the week. Everything above is in the [vegetables aisle](/shop/vegetables) and the [frozen vegetables aisle](/shop/frozen-veg), sold in quantities that suit one.

posts.title: Our growers: the Vale orchard, twelve years on
posts.excerpt: One family, four hundred trees and a harvest that still moves entirely by hand.
posts.body:
The Vale orchard sits at the bottom of a sheltered valley, on a slope that faces south and catches the afternoon sun. It is not large. There are four hundred trees across a little over three hectares, most of them apples, with two long rows of pears along the lower hedge. The same family has worked it for three generations, and for the past twelve years every apple and pear they pick by hand has come to our shelves. This is the story of how a small orchard has stayed small on purpose, and why its harvest still happens one piece of fruit at a time.

## One family, three generations

Ruth Vale planted the first rows in the 1970s, on land that had been grazing pasture. Her son Tom took over in the nineties and replaced the tall old standard trees with smaller trees on dwarfing rootstocks, which bear fruit sooner and can be picked from the ground or a short ladder. Today Tom and his daughter Hannah run the orchard between them, with Ruth still walking the rows most mornings and offering opinions on the pruning.

When our buyers first met them, the Vales were selling most of their crop to a wholesaler who blended it with fruit from dozens of other farms. The fruit was good. It simply disappeared into a bigger pile. The arrangement we agreed that first autumn was simple: we would take a fixed share of the harvest at a price agreed before picking began, and the Vale name would stay on the crate. Twelve seasons later, that is still the deal.

![A grower in a greenhouse holding a crate of fresh produce](/images/home-promos/maintain-fitness.jpg "Between harvests the work is tending: pruning, thinning and checking every row.")

## Four hundred trees, counted one by one

At this size, Hannah knows the orchard tree by tree. She keeps a notebook for each row with notes on blossom, fruit set, disease and yield. The trees are numbered, and the older ones have names.

That attention shows up in the fruit. A small orchard can thin by hand in early summer, removing some of the young fruit so that the rest grows larger and sweeter. It can prune each tree to let light into its centre, where colour and sugar develop. And it can walk every row after a storm to check for damage, which on a large estate would take days.

Pollination is shared work. A beekeeper from the next village keeps a dozen hives along the top hedge each spring, and the bees work the blossom for the few weeks it is open. The Vales count on them for a good fruit set, and the beekeeper counts on the orchard for a light, floral spring honey. It is the kind of arrangement that only works when both sides plan to be there next year.

The Vales grow several apple varieties, picked over a long season, and two varieties of pear. Our shelves carry Pink Lady apples and Conference pears from their best rows in a good year, alongside fruit from other trusted growers when the Vale crop runs out.

{{products: pink-lady-apples, conference-pears}}

## A harvest that still moves by hand

Apples bruise easily, and a bruise that is invisible on picking day turns brown a week later. So nothing at Vale is shaken from a tree or gathered from the ground for sale. Every fruit is picked by hand.

The pickers wear a canvas bag across the chest with an opening at the bottom. Each apple is lifted and turned upward so the stalk comes away cleanly, then placed, not dropped, into the bag. When the bag is full, its bottom opens into a wooden bin, and the fruit rolls gently out. A good picker can fill a bin in a morning.

Not every apple on a tree ripens on the same day. The fruit on the sunny, outside branches is ready first. So each row is picked two or three times, a week or so apart, taking only the fruit that is ready. Pink Lady is one of the last apples of the season to ripen, and its picking often runs well into late autumn.

> "You can't hurry an apple. You just go back and ask it again next week." — Tom Vale

Pears are handled differently. Conference pears are picked while still firm and green, when they lift easily from the branch. They ripen off the tree, in cool storage and then in your fruit bowl. A pear left to soften on the branch tends to turn grainy at the core.

## What twelve years have changed

The trees have changed. When we started, about a third of the orchard was old trees that cropped every other year. Tom has replanted in stages, a row or two each winter, so the orchard never loses its whole crop to replanting at once.

The way the fruit is stored has changed, too. With help from a long-term buying agreement, the Vales invested in a small cold store, which keeps apples at a steady low temperature after picking. That slows their ripening, so fruit picked in October can still be crisp weeks later. It also means the fruit leaves the farm in better condition, which is one of the reasons it arrives on our shelves tasting the way it does. There is more on this in [the cold chain, explained in plain language](/journal/the-cold-chain-explained-in-plain-language).

What has not changed is the scale. The Vales have been offered more land more than once. They have said no each time. Four hundred trees is what one family can know properly, and they would rather know every tree than grow twice as many.

![A picker at harvest holding a basket in a sunlit field](/images/home-promos/keep-active.jpg "Picking season still moves one basket at a time.")

## How to get the best from their fruit

Fruit picked this carefully deserves careful keeping at home:

- **Apples** stay crisp much longer in the fridge than in a fruit bowl. Keep a few out to eat that day and the rest in the salad drawer.
- **Pears** should ripen at room temperature. Check the neck, near the stalk: when it gives slightly to gentle pressure, the pear is ready. Then move it to the fridge and eat it within a couple of days.
- **Keep apples away from other produce** in the bowl if you want it to last. Ripening apples give off ethylene, a gas that speeds up ripening in fruit and vegetables nearby.

## Taste the difference this autumn

When Vale fruit is in season, it is marked with the orchard's name in the [orchard fruit aisle](/shop/orchard). Buy a few apples and a couple of pears, keep them the way the Vales would, then eat one side by side with an apple from somewhere else and see whether you notice the difference.

posts.title: The freezer is not a graveyard
posts.excerpt: A labelling system that takes ten seconds and rescues about thirty dollars a week.
posts.body:
Every freezer has a back corner where food goes to be forgotten. A foil parcel with no name. A bag of something brown that might be chilli and might be stew. Half a loaf from a month nobody remembers. Most of it was perfectly good when it went in, and most of it will be thrown out when it finally comes back out. The fix is not a bigger freezer or a stricter plan. It is a label that takes ten seconds to write, and a way of stacking that makes the oldest food the easiest to reach.

## Why freezers turn into graveyards

Food does not go bad in a freezer kept at −18 °C. Freezing stops the growth of the bacteria that make food unsafe, so frozen food stays safe for a very long time. What it loses is quality. Over months, ice crystals damage texture, air dries out the surface into pale "freezer burn", and flavours fade.

So the problem is rarely safety. It is that we cannot tell what something is or how long it has been there. Faced with a mystery bag, most of us leave it where it is and cook something else. By the time we look again, it has been there a year, and in the bin it goes.

> A freezer does not waste food. Forgetting what is in it does.

## The ten-second label

Every bag or box that goes into the freezer gets three things, written on a strip of masking tape with a permanent marker:

1. **What it is, and how much.** "Chicken thigh x2", "Lentil soup, 1 portion", "Bread, 6 slices". Be specific enough that you could plan a meal from the label alone.
2. **The date it went in.** Day and month is enough.
3. **An "eat by" month.** Your own target for best quality, not a safety date.

That is it. Masking tape sticks to cold plastic, peels off cleanly and costs very little. Keep a roll and a marker in the drawer nearest the freezer, so labelling happens at the same moment as freezing. If you have to go and find a pen, you will skip it.

> **Tip:** Write the "eat by" month bigger than everything else. It is the one line you need to read at a glance with the door open.

For the "eat by" month, these are sensible targets for home freezers:

- **Bread, cakes and pastry:** within 3 months.
- **Cooked dishes, soups and sauces:** within 3 months.
- **Raw fish and prawns:** within 3 months for the best texture.
- **Raw chicken, sausages and minced meat:** within 3 to 4 months.
- **Raw joints and steaks:** within 6 months.
- **Frozen vegetables and fruit:** follow the "best before" on the pack. These are frozen quickly after harvest and keep their quality well.

{{products: frozen-garden-peas, frozen-mixed-berries}}

## Stack it so the oldest comes first

A label only helps if you can see it. Two simple layout rules make the difference:

- **Freeze flat, then file upright.** Fill bags about two thirds full, press out the air and freeze them flat on a tray. Once solid, stand them upright in a drawer like files in a cabinet, labels facing up. You can read every one without moving anything.
- **New goes to the back.** When you add something, move the older items forward. The front of each drawer is always "eat this next".

Give each drawer a job if you can: one for raw meat and fish, one for cooked meals, one for bread, vegetables and fruit. Raw meat and fish should sit below ready-to-eat food, in sealed bags, so nothing drips onto something you will not cook again.

![A canvas tote of vegetables and fruit with a bottle of produce wash](/images/blog/journal-04.jpg "Portion and label on the day you shop, while everything is at its freshest.")

## Freezing and thawing, safely

### Putting it in

Portion before you freeze, not after. A single block of eight chicken thighs is useless on a night you want two. Freeze in the amounts you actually cook.

- **Meat and fish:** freeze on the day you buy it, well before its "use by" date. Portion into single meals and freeze flat.
- **Bread:** slice first. Toast straight from frozen.
- **Cooked food:** cool it quickly and get it into the freezer within two hours of cooking. Shallow containers cool faster than deep ones.
- **Ripe bananas:** peel, slice and freeze on a tray for smoothies and baking.
- **Grated cheese:** freeze in a bag and use straight from frozen on pasta or toast.

{{products: chicken-thigh-fillets, outdoor-pork-sausages}}

### Taking it back out

A good label tells you what to take out the night before. The safest way to thaw is slowly, in the fridge, on a plate to catch any liquid. Most portions thaw overnight. Never thaw raw meat or fish on the kitchen counter.

Some food can be cooked straight from frozen. Frozen vegetables, prawns and thin fish fillets go straight into the pan or oven. Sausages can be cooked from frozen if you cook them longer and check they are piping hot in the middle. Reheated leftovers should also be piping hot all the way through.

> **Watch out:** Once raw meat or fish has thawed, do not refreeze it raw. Cook it first, cool it, and then you can freeze the cooked dish.

{{products: raw-king-prawns}}

## The five-minute weekly check

Once a week, before you write your shopping list, open the freezer and read the front row of each drawer. Anything with this month's "eat by" goes onto the week's meal plan first. It takes a few minutes, and it turns the freezer from a store room into a second larder.

How much this saves depends on your household. The figure in the headline is a rough estimate for a family that regularly throws out frozen food, and your own number could be higher or lower. The simplest way to find out is to keep a note for a month of everything you would once have binned.

![A delivery of fresh groceries handed over at the door](/images/blog/journal-07.jpg "Check the freezer before you order, and the shop gets smaller.")

## Start with one roll of tape

Tonight, put a roll of masking tape and a marker next to the freezer. Label the next thing you put in, and the one after that. Within a few weeks the mystery bags will be gone. For more ideas on stretching what you already have, read [meal planning for a household of one](/journal/meal-planning-for-a-household-of-one), and browse the [frozen vegetables aisle](/shop/frozen-veg) for the staples that make the freezer work hardest.

posts.title: Breakfast that survives a weekday morning
posts.excerpt: Five assemblies, none of them requiring a pan or a decision before coffee.
posts.body:
Weekday breakfast fails for two reasons, and neither of them is a lack of food. The first is effort: anything that needs a pan, a hob and a wash-up loses to the clock. The second is choice: standing at the open fridge at seven in the morning, deciding what to eat, is how most people end up eating nothing. The five breakfasts below solve both. None of them uses a pan. Each one is assembled in under five minutes, or put together the night before. And because each has its own day, there is nothing to decide before coffee.

## The rules that make it work

Three principles sit behind every one of these breakfasts:

- **Assemble, do not cook.** A bowl, a knife, a toaster at most. If it needs a pan, it belongs on a weekend.
- **Give each breakfast a day.** A fixed rota removes the decision. Monday is always the same, and so is Tuesday. You can swap days when you feel like it, but you never have to.
- **Shop for the rota.** Once a week, buy what the five breakfasts need and nothing else for the morning. The fridge then holds the answer before you open it.

Each breakfast combines something slow-burning, such as oats, bread or nuts, with fruit and some protein. For many people that tends to feel more filling through the morning than sugary cereal alone, though everyone is different.

![A paper grocery bag spilling tomatoes, carrots, bread and milk](/images/blog/journal-01.jpg "One weekly shop covers all five mornings.")

## The five assemblies

### 1. Monday: overnight oats with blueberries and honey

Made on Sunday night in a jar or a lidded bowl. Stir together half a cup of jumbo rolled oats and about three quarters of a cup of milk or yoghurt, then add a pinch of salt. Put the lid on and leave it in the fridge. In the morning the oats have softened into something creamy and thick. Top with a handful of blueberries, a spoonful of honey and a few walnut halves.

Jumbo oats are best here. They hold their shape overnight instead of turning to paste. Make two jars at once and Tuesday's breakfast is ready too, if you want it.

{{products: jumbo-rolled-oats, wild-blueberries, runny-blossom-honey}}

### 2. Tuesday: avocado toast with tomato and lime

The toaster is the only appliance. While the bread toasts, halve a ripe avocado and slice a tomato. Mash the avocado straight onto the toast with a fork, lay the tomato over it, add salt, pepper and a good squeeze of lime. A drizzle of olive oil is worth it if you have it.

Buy avocados at different stages of ripeness so one is always ready. A ripe Hass avocado gives slightly when you press gently near the stalk. Keep ripe ones in the fridge to slow them down.

{{products: hass-avocados, juicy-vine-tomatoes, persian-limes}}

### 3. Wednesday: the cheese, apple and walnut plate

A breakfast that needs only a board and a knife. Slice an apple, cut a few slices of mature cheddar and add a small handful of walnuts. Add a piece of bread or a couple of oatcakes if you are hungry. It sounds more like lunch than breakfast, but sweet fruit and sharp cheese are a very old pairing, and it keeps well in a lunchbox if you have to eat on the way.

{{products: pink-lady-apples, mature-cheddar, california-walnut-halves}}

### 4. Thursday: the green smoothie that does not taste green

A blender is not a pan, and this takes about two minutes. Blend one banana, a peeled kiwi, a large handful of baby spinach, two tablespoons of oats and a glass of milk. The banana and kiwi cover the taste of the spinach almost completely, and the oats make it thick and filling.

For a colder smoothie, peel and slice ripe bananas at the weekend and freeze them on a tray. Wash the blender jug straight away, while it takes seconds.

{{products: cavendish-bananas, ripe-kiwis, baby-leaf-spinach}}

### 5. Friday: yoghurt, pear and honey bowl

The easiest of the five. Spoon thick yoghurt into a bowl, slice a ripe pear over it, drizzle with honey and finish with crushed walnuts. A ripe pear should give a little near the stalk. If the pears are still firm on Monday, leave them in the fruit bowl and they should be ready by Friday.

![A smiling woman holding a double handful of fruit and vegetables](/images/editorial/handful-of-produce.jpg "Fruit bought for a plan gets eaten. Fruit bought on a whim often does not.")

## The Sunday ten minutes

A little preparation on Sunday makes the whole week easier:

1. Make Monday's overnight oats, or two jars of them.
2. Check the avocados and pears. Move ripe ones to the fridge and leave firm ones out.
3. Wash and dry the blueberries only when you are ready to eat them. Stored wet, they spoil faster.
4. Put walnuts in a small jar next to the kettle, so they are within reach for three of the five breakfasts.

Keep the fridge at or below 5 °C and eat overnight oats within two days. Keep milk, yoghurt and cheese on a shelf, not in the door, where the temperature changes each time it opens.

> **Tip:** Write the rota on a sticky note inside a cupboard door. It sounds too simple to matter, but it is the note, not your memory, that makes the decision at seven in the morning.

## Your shopping list for the week

Everything for the five breakfasts, for one person:

- Jumbo rolled oats, milk and thick yoghurt
- A punnet of blueberries
- Two avocados, two tomatoes and a lime
- Two apples, two pears, two bananas and a kiwi
- A bag of baby spinach
- A block of mature cheddar and a loaf of bread
- Walnut halves and a jar of honey

For more ways to plan a week of eating without repeating yourself, see [weekly grocery list: what to buy for a healthy lifestyle](/journal/weekly-grocery-list-what-to-buy-for-a-healthy-lifestyle).

## Start on Sunday night

This Sunday, make one jar of overnight oats and write the rota on a note. Monday morning will already be decided. Pick up the fruit from the [fruits aisle](/shop/fruits) and the oats from [oats and cereals](/shop/oats-cereals), and see whether the week feels easier by Friday.
